accroche: Feyerabend argues that Galileo never followed the scientific method attributed to him, and that this is precisely what allowed him to prevail.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1975, the Austrian philosopher Paul Feyerabend published *Against Method: Outline of an Anarchistic Theory of Knowledge*. His central thesis fits in one sentence: no universal methodological rule has ever really governed the scientific advances of the past, and imposing one today would freeze progress rather than guarantee it.

## The mechanism

Feyerabend builds his demonstration on specific historical cases, foremost among them Galileo's defense of heliocentrism. The received image has Galileo triumphing through the sheer force of telescopic observation and logical reasoning. Feyerabend points out that things are less clear-cut: the telescope was, at the time, a contested instrument, whose optical reliability was itself debated among scholars, and a physical objection remained without a solid answer for decades, the tower argument: an object dropped from the top of a tower should, if the Earth rotates, fall behind, something no experiment of the period could verify with certainty. Feyerabend argues that Galileo prevailed less through rigorous demonstration in the sense we understand it today than through rhetoric, the skillful reinterpretation of common experience, and a good dose of what he calls, bluntly, propaganda, making his position intuitively appealing rather than strictly proven according to the canons that would be attributed to him after the fact.

## What this shifts

Hence the slogan that stayed attached to his name: the only rule that never hinders progress is that there is none, “anything goes.” Feyerabend nonetheless specifies that this slogan is not an invitation to anything-goes-whatever, but a historical observation: every methodological rule that people have tried to erect into a universal criterion, strict induction, confrontation with facts alone, the rejection of any ad hoc hypothesis, is violated by at least one major episode that is nonetheless considered, in retrospect, an indisputable scientific advance.

Feyerabend thus extends, while radicalizing it, a line already present in this collection: the Duhem–Quine thesis, which shows that an anomaly never singles out by itself what has to be revised, and Kuhn's revolutions, in which the passage from one paradigm to another follows no logic of progressive confirmation. Where Kuhn describes a historical phenomenon without drawing a radical normative consequence from it, Feyerabend goes further and denies that a single method has ever existed, or should exist. His position remains debated, and largely a minority one among philosophers of science; in the 1990s it fed what came to be called the “science wars,” a clash between scientists and a part of the philosophy of science over the epistemic authority to grant to the scientific method itself. It remains, to this day, the most openly provocative position in the whole discipline that studies how science produces what it knows.

citation.texte: The only principle that does not inhibit progress is: anything goes.
citation.source: Against Method: Outline of an Anarchistic Theory of Knowledge, New Left Books, 1975, Introduction

carte.punch: No universal scientific rule has ever withstood examination against its own past.
carte.idee: Feyerabend argues, in 1975, that Galileo defended heliocentrism through rhetoric and propaganda, not through a strict scientific method, at a time when the telescope was contested and the tower objection unanswered. Hence his slogan: “anything goes.”

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Paul Feyerabend
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A full presentation of his thought and of the debates it has stirred.

quiz.question: What does Feyerabend really mean by his slogan “anything goes”?
choix: That every scientific claim is equally valid, whether verified or not
That no fixed methodological rule withstands examination against real cases
That science should stop trying to verify its hypotheses
That Galileo was fundamentally wrong to defend heliocentrism
quiz.explication: Feyerabend himself specifies that his slogan is not an invitation to treat everything as equally valid: he observes that every methodological rule erected into a universal criterion has been violated by at least one episode considered in retrospect a major scientific advance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which historical case does Feyerabend develop at length in Against Method?
choix: The debate between Pasteur and his contemporaries over spontaneous generation
Darwin's formulation of the theory of evolution
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Feyerabend devotes a large part of his book to Galileo, to show that his scientific victory is not explained by adherence to a strict method, but by rhetoric and the reinterpretation of common experience.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why, according to Feyerabend, is Galileo's use of the telescope not enough to explain his victory?
choix: Because Galileo never actually used an astronomical telescope
Because the optical reliability of the instrument was itself contested at the time
Because the telescope was invented only after Galileo's death
Because the Church formally forbade its use in astronomy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In Galileo's day, the telescope was an instrument whose optical reliability was debated among scholars: its use alone was therefore not enough to win conviction according to the canons of proof that would later be attributed to the scientific method.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which debate of the 1990s did Feyerabend's position feed?
choix: The debate over dating the age of the universe
The “science wars,” over the epistemic authority of the scientific method
The debate over French spelling reform
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Feyerabend's epistemological anarchism contributed, in the 1990s, to the “science wars,” a clash between scientists and a part of the philosophy of science over the authority to grant to the scientific method.
